problem: According to the rational roots theorem, which of the following **cannot** be a root of the polynomial $f(x)=14{x}^{4}+3{x}^{2}-x-7?$
worked_solution:
Given a polynomial with integer coefficients, the rational roots theorem states that any rational roots of the polynomial must take the form

$$
\pm \frac{\text{factor of the constant term}}{\text{factor of the leading coefficient}}.
$$

For the given polynomial $f(x),$ the constant term is $-7$ and the leading coefficient is $14.$ So, any rational roots of $f(x)$ must take the form

$$
\pm \frac{\text{factor of }-7}{\text{factor of }14}.
$$

Of the given answer choices, only $\frac{1}{21}$ does not take the above form. The denominator $(21)$ is not a factor of $14.$

The given points are ${{(2,2)}_{⏟}}_{\text{(}{x}_{1},\,{y}_{1})}$, ${{(a,b)}_{⏟}}_{\text{(}{x}_{2},\,{y}_{2})}$ and ${{(-1,4)}_{⏟}}_{\text{(}{x}_{m},\,{y}_{m})}.$

We use the midpoint formula as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}({x}_{m},{y}_{m}) & =(\frac{{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}}{2},\frac{{y}_{1}+{y}_{2}}{2}) \\ (-1,4) & =(\frac{2+a}{2},\frac{2+b}{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding $x$- and $y$-coordinates in the equation above gives us

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}-1=\frac{2+a}{2} \\ 4=\frac{2+b}{2}\end{aligned}\,⇒\,{\begin{aligned}a=-4 \\ b=6.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $(a,b)=(-4,6).$
